newsitem.title: USA: Fund expenses still matter to investors.
newsitem.headline: Fund expenses still matter to investors.

text.p: When stock and bond prices are rising, few investors give much thought to mutual fund expenses. But that could change suddenly if the financial markets stumble.
The annual expenses and transaction fees on a fund could make the difference between making and losing money in a mediocre year for the markets.

For example, back in 1994 the S&P 500 index gained 1.3 percent -- but the average fund's expenses amounted to 1.45 percent of each shareholders' investment. Thus, it was quite easy to lose money even if your fund matched the index's return.

Some shareholders are inclined to accept fund expenses as a necessary evil while others don't even give them a thought. But you can take action to reduce your investment expenses with results that could be terrific for your financial health.

Let's say you reduce your retirement portfolio's annual expenses from 1.8 percent to 1.3 percent -- boosting your take-home return from 8.5 percent to 9 percent annually. If you start with $25,000, your money will grow to $215,577 over 25 years. That compares to only $192,169 if you had swallowed the higher expenses.

Such examples don't account for transaction costs such as loads -- initial sales charges that you will often pay when you buy a fund through a broker, financial planner or other middle man, rather than buying directly from no-load fund companies.
These charges often amount to 3 percent or more of your initial investment. Thus, it only makes sense to pay these charges if you need the broker's or planner's advice to make your fund choices.

Before you invest in a fund, you should at least know what your expense money buys. Every fund has an expense ratio, which equals the percentage of shareholders' assets that go to pay fund expenses each year.

The money may be used for several purposes. First, it goes to pay a "management fee" to the company that chooses stocks, bonds or other securities for the fund. It also covers other expenses such as record-keeping, prospectuses and the like.

Finally, many funds' expenses include a 12b-1 fee, which usually goes to brokers or financial planners who sell you the shares. Even funds that also charge an initial sales commission sometimes add a 12b-1 fee, so that your broker will continue to get money every year that you own the fund.
Expenses are most important when you are choosing between two funds with similar risks and investment objectives. That often happens with fixed-income funds.

For example, two funds that invest in mortgage-backed securities might offer little difference in strategy or potential investment returns. Thus, the one with higher expenses will likely deliver less profit.
What's more, a small difference in annual returns might make a big difference to bond investors.

USAA GNMA Fund (800-382-8722; $3,000 minimum investment; no-load) and Lexington GNMA Income Fund (800-526-0056; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load) both invest most of their assets in GNMA certificates. But the Lexington fund has an expense ratio of 1.01 percent, compared with an expense ratio of only 0.32 percent for the USAA fund.

Assuming that the two funds have identical investment returns of 6 percent over the next year, the USAA GNMA Fund will generate a 5.68 percent return after expenses, compared with a 4.99 percent return for the Lexington GNMA Income Fund.

That performance gap may not sound like much. But at those rates, a $10,000 investment in the USAA GNMA Fund will grow to $30,189 over 20 years, compared to only $26,482 for a similar investment in the Lexington GNMA Fund.

Among actively managed stock funds, such differences might matter less, and you will probably encounter fewer funds that are almost identical in terms of their investment strategies. But passively-managed index funds are another matter.

Take Vanguard Index 500 Fund (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum investment; no-load) and Dreyfus S&P 500 Fund (800-645-6561; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load). Both funds seek to mirror the performance of the Standard and Poor's 500 Index.

However, Vanguard's offering has an expense ratio of 0.20 percent, vs. a 0.53 percent expense ratio for the Dreyfus fund. Assuming both funds gain 10 percent during the next year, Vanguard Index 500's real return after expenses will be 9.8 percent, compared with a 9.47 percent return on Dreyfus S&P 500 Fund.

At those returns, a $10,000 investment in Vanguard Index 500 will grow to $165,222 in 30 years, while the same investment in Dreyfus S&P 500 will only grow to $150,957 -- a $14,265 difference. That's a pretty sizable incentive to pay more attention to fund expenses.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
